question: What is @ParameterizedTest and what sources can you use?
title: @ParameterizedTest JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **`@ParameterizedTest`** runs the same test body once per input set, replacing copy-pasted near-identical tests. You feed data with a **source**: `@ValueSource` (single literals), `@CsvSource` (input→expected rows), `@MethodSource` (a `Stream<Arguments>` for complex objects), plus `@EnumSource`, `@NullSource`, and `@CsvFileSource`. It needs the `junit-jupiter-params` module.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`@ParameterizedTest`** replaces `@Test` for data-driven tests.
- **`@ValueSource`** — one literal per run.
- **`@CsvSource`** — input→expected rows with supported conversion.
- **`@MethodSource`** — typed objects or computed arguments from a factory; a local factory is normally static under `PER_METHOD`.
- **Each argument set** is a separate reported invocation; name it with `@ParameterizedTest(name = ...)`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A parameterized test runs the same test body against several argument sets. I annotate the method with `@ParameterizedTest` and attach a source.

`@ValueSource` supplies one simple value per invocation. `@CsvSource` is useful for a small input-and-expected table and applies supported text conversions. `@MethodSource` supplies typed or computed data from Java code; a local factory is static under the default `PER_METHOD` lifecycle, while `PER_CLASS` allows an instance factory. An external factory remains static. Other choices include enum, null, empty, and CSV-file sources.

Each argument set appears as a separate invocation in the report. The `name` attribute belongs on `@ParameterizedTest` and can include indexes or argument values. Use separate tests when cases no longer share the same behavior and assertion shape.

sections.title: Match the argument source to the shape of the data
sections.content:
**`@ParameterizedTest`** marks a reusable test template. An argument-source annotation supplies the values, and JUnit runs the template once for every supplied case. This keeps the behavior in one place while showing the set of examples clearly in the test report.

For example, `@ValueSource(ints = {2, 4, 8})` is suitable for one integer parameter. Use `@CsvSource` when each case has several simple columns, `@MethodSource` for objects or computed data, `@EnumSource` for enum values, and `@NullSource` or `@EmptySource` for those edge cases. The source is part of the test design: choosing a complex factory for two simple values makes the test harder to read, while forcing objects into CSV strings makes it fragile.

sections.title: How Sources Feed the Test
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB V["@ValueSource
single literals"] --> E["@ParameterizedTest
method"] C["@CsvSource
input -> expected"] --> E M["@MethodSource
Stream"] --> E E --> R["runs once per row,
each a reported case"] ```

sections.title: The Common Sources
Which Source to Use
sections.content:
| Source | Best for | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `@ValueSource` | One argument, simple literals | a list of ints/strings |
| `@CsvSource` | Input→expected pairs inline | `"2, 3, 5"` |
| `@CsvFileSource` | Many rows from a file | `data.csv` |
| `@MethodSource` | Complex objects or computed data | `Stream<Arguments>` |
| `@EnumSource` | All or selected enum constants | `Status.class` |
| `@NullSource`/`@EmptySource` | null or empty edge cases | strings and supported types |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `@Test`.** Parameters won't be injected; you need `@ParameterizedTest`.
- **Wrong source.** `@ValueSource` carries only one argument; use `@CsvSource` for pairs.
- **Non-static `@MethodSource`.** Factory must be `static` unless using `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)`.
- **Missing module.** Needs `junit-jupiter-params` (already in `spring-boot-starter-test`).

question: How do you use @CsvSource for testing multiple input-output pairs?
title: @CsvSource JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **`@CsvSource`** supplies inline delimiter-separated rows to a `@ParameterizedTest`. Each column maps to a method parameter and JUnit performs supported conversions. With the default settings, an unquoted empty column becomes `null`, while `''` is an empty string; `nullValues` and `emptyValue` customize those meanings. Quote values containing the delimiter and use the parameterized test's `name` for readable reports.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`@CsvSource`** — inline delimiter-separated argument rows.
- **Supported conversion** — columns can convert to ints, enums, booleans, and other supported targets.
- **Quote delimiters** inside a value with the configured quote character.
- **Default empty rules** — unquoted empty is null; `''` is an empty String.
- **Invocation name** — set `name` on @ParameterizedTest to label each row.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
CsvSource puts a small argument table next to a parameterized test. Each row becomes one invocation, columns map by position, and JUnit performs supported conversion to types such as int, boolean, enum, or BigDecimal. For a password validator, rows can pair a password with the expected valid flag.

The empty-value rules matter: with default settings, an **unquoted empty column is null**, while `''` produces an empty String. `nullValues` can name tokens that should become null, and `emptyValue` changes the value produced by a quoted empty field. A value containing the delimiter must be quoted with the configured quote character. The invocation display name belongs on `@ParameterizedTest(name = ...)`, not on @CsvSource.

sections.title: Each CSV row maps to one invocation
sections.content:
**`@CsvSource`** keeps a small table of simple arguments beside a parameterized test. JUnit splits each row into columns, converts supported text values to the method parameter types, and runs the method once per row.

For example, `"2, 3, 5"` can supply `int left, int right, int expected`. With defaults, `"apple,"` supplies null for the second column, while `"apple, ''"` supplies an empty string. Use `nullValues` for named null tokens and `emptyValue` to customize a quoted empty field. Put a custom invocation name on @ParameterizedTest. Use @MethodSource when cases need rich objects or setup logic.

sections.title: @CsvSource at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Shape|~Comma rows|each row = one run|cells map to params|positional
blue|Conversion|~Automatic|String -> int/enum|boolean, BigDecimal|no manual parsing
amber|Edge cases|~null & empty|nullValues = "null"|emptyValue|quote commas
violet|Reports|~name pattern|name = "{0} -> {1}"|readable cases|labelled rows

sections.title: Repetitive: one test per case
Compact: one @CsvSource table
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Unquoted delimiter.** A value like `1,000` splits into two cells unless quoted as `'1,000'` with the default quote character.
- **Reversing null and empty.** An unquoted empty column is null by default; `''` is an empty String.
- **Assuming every conversion exists.** Built-in and registered converters handle many types; use an argument converter or MethodSource when needed.
- **Putting `name` on the source.** Invocation naming is configured on @ParameterizedTest.

question: How do you test boundary conditions using parameterized tests?
title: Boundary Condition Testing JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: Boundary testing checks the edges where bugs cluster: for a valid range `[min, max]`, test **min-1, min, max, max+1** (and often 0, empty, and null). Parameterized tests express this as a compact table so you systematically cover the boundaries instead of one happy-path value — most off-by-one bugs live exactly at these edges.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Bugs cluster at edges** — boundaries, not the middle.
- **Recipe** — min-1, min, max, max+1 (plus a mid value).
- **Specials** — 0, empty, null, overflow.
- **Parameterized table** covers all edges in one test.
- **Pairs with** equivalence partitioning.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The core idea behind boundary testing is that bugs cluster at the edges of a valid range, not in the middle. Most of them are off-by-one errors — using less-than where you meant less-than-or-equal, that kind of thing. So testing one value in the middle of the range proves almost nothing about where the bugs actually live.

The technique is boundary value analysis. For a valid range from min to max, I test four key points: just below min, exactly min, exactly max, and just above max. I usually throw in a clearly valid middle value too. So if a rule says an age has to be between eighteen and sixty-five inclusive, I'd test seventeen as invalid, eighteen as valid, sixty-five as valid, and sixty-six as invalid. The seventeen and sixty-six cases are what catch the off-by-one mistakes. I'd also add special cases that often break on their own — zero, negative numbers, empty strings, null, and overflow values like Integer max.

Parameterized tests are the perfect tool for this, because I can put all those edges into a single CsvSource table and run one test body against all of them. That makes the coverage systematic and easy to read, and adding a boundary is just another row. I give it a name pattern so each row is labelled, because when a boundary fails I want to know immediately which one.

This pairs with equivalence partitioning, where I group inputs into classes — invalid-low, valid, invalid-high — and pick representatives, then focus on the edges between them.

sections.title: Turn every boundary into a visible data row
sections.content:
Boundary testing checks values where behavior changes, because off-by-one mistakes usually live there. For an inclusive range `[min, max]`, useful cases are just below `min`, exactly `min`, just above `min`, one ordinary value, just below `max`, exactly `max`, and just above `max`.

For example, an age rule accepting 18 through 65 can use `@CsvSource` rows for `17,false`, `18,true`, `19,true`, `64,true`, `65,true`, and `66,false`. The expected result belongs in the same row, so every decision is visible. Invalid-input cases that should throw can use a separate parameterized test with `assertThrows`. Do not generate many random middle values while omitting the edges; the boundary points carry the most information.

sections.title: Boundary Recipe for [min, max]
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A["min - 1
(invalid)"] --> B["min
(valid edge)"] B --> C["mid
(valid)"] C --> D["max
(valid edge)"] D --> E["max + 1
(invalid)"] ```

sections.title: Boundary Table with @CsvSource
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **One value only.** Testing age 40 proves nothing about the 18/65 edges where off-by-one bugs live.
- **Skipping just-outside.** min-1 and max+1 catch `<` vs `<=` mistakes.
- **Ignoring specials.** 0, empty string, null, and overflow values often break separately.
- **Vague labels.** Without a `name` pattern, a failing boundary row is hard to identify.

question: How do you use @MethodSource for complex parameterized test arguments?
title: @MethodSource JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **`@MethodSource`** supplies arguments from a factory method. A multi-argument factory commonly returns **`Stream<Arguments>`**, while Jupiter also accepts other supported stream-like return types. Use it for typed objects, computed cases, or reusable data. A factory in the test class is normally static under `PER_METHOD`; `PER_CLASS` allows an instance factory. A factory in an external class must be static.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`@MethodSource`** — factory supplying one or more argument sets.
- **`Arguments.of(...)`** — one invocation with several typed parameters.
- **Local factory** — static under `PER_METHOD`; an instance factory is allowed under `PER_CLASS`.
- **For rich data** — objects, nulls, computed values, or reusable cases.
- **External factory** — reference it as `Class#method`; it must be static.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
MethodSource is the parameterized source I use when the arguments are too rich for CSV. Instead of inline strings, I point it at a factory method that returns a Stream of Arguments, and each Arguments dot of call becomes one run of the test, with the elements mapped to the test's parameters.

The reason I'd choose it over CsvSource is when my inputs are real domain objects, computed values, or include nulls — things you can't cleanly express as comma-separated text. For example, testing a pricing service, my factory can produce a premium customer with a hundred dollar order expecting ninety, a regular customer expecting a hundred, and an edge case with a zero order. Each of those is an Arguments dot of with actual objects, which is much clearer than trying to encode them as strings.

There are a couple of rules. The factory method has to be static by default — if I want it non-static, I switch the class to the per-class test instance lifecycle. And if I leave the MethodSource value blank, it looks for a method with the same name as the test; otherwise I name it explicitly. A nice feature is that I can also reference a factory in a completely different class using its fully-qualified name with a hash before the method name, which is great for sharing test data across classes.

Common mistakes are forgetting the static requirement, getting the method name wrong, and reaching for MethodSource when a simple ValueSource or CsvSource would do.

sections.title: A factory method supplies rich test arguments
sections.content:
**`@MethodSource`** connects a parameterized test to a factory method that supplies argument sets. It is useful when inline annotations would make the data hard to read—for example, when each case contains an `Order`, a `CustomerType`, and an expected `BigDecimal`. The factory commonly returns `Stream<Arguments>`, although Jupiter supports several stream-like forms.

For example, `static Stream<Arguments> discountCases()` can return cases through `Arguments.of(...)`, and `@MethodSource("discountCases")` feeds them to the test. If the annotation has no value, JUnit looks for a factory with the same name as the test method. A local factory is static under the default per-method lifecycle, while `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)` allows it to be an instance method. A factory referenced from another class must remain static. Keep the data readable and deterministic.

sections.title: @MethodSource at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|What it is|~Factory method|returns Stream<Arguments>|each = one run|rich data
blue|Build args|~Arguments.of(...)|typed objects|mixed types|nulls OK
amber|Rules|~static by default|name matches if blank|PER_CLASS for non-static|external via FQN
violet|Use when|~CSV too limited|domain objects|computed values|complex combos

sections.title: Complex Objects via @MethodSource
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Non-static local factory under `PER_METHOD`.** Use `static` or select `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)`. External factory methods must be static.
- **Name mismatch.** Blank `@MethodSource` defaults to a method named like the test; otherwise name it explicitly.
- **Unnecessary complexity.** For simple literals or pairs, `@ValueSource`/`@CsvSource` are often clearer.
- **Argument shape mismatch.** Make each emitted item match the test method's parameter list; use `Arguments.of(...)` for several parameters.
